subject: Biology
title: Plant Kingdom
summary: A tour of the five major plant groups in evolutionary order, algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, with the structure, reproduction, examples and economic use of each, ending with the three patterns of plant life cycle. It is a memory-heavy chapter: NCERT names, pigments, stored foods, flagella, ploidy and labelled diagrams decide the marks, and the same facts return in Class 12 (Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants) and in NEET every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school. Plant Kingdom sits in Unit I, Diversity of Living World, which carries 15 marks shared with The Living World, Biological Classification and Animal Kingdom. In a typical school final this chapter contributes about 4 to 6 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ or an Assertion–Reason), a 2-mark or 3-mark question, and in some papers a 5-mark question on gymnosperms, bryophyte or pteridophyte life cycle, or alternation of generations. In NEET it is one of the most reliable chapters, with two to three questions almost every year drawn word-for-word from NCERT.

question_types.note: Match a pigment, stored food or flagella pattern to an algal class; pick the heterosporous pteridophyte; identify the ploidy of protonema, prothallus, endosperm or gemma; spot the example (Sequoia, Wolffia, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, Chara, Salvinia); anisogamy versus oogamy; where meiosis happens in a fern or a moss; which group has no free-living gametophyte.

Bryophytes as amphibians of the plant kingdom; gymnosperm ovules being naked; heterospory as a precursor to the seed habit; the sporophyte in mosses depending on the gametophyte; Fucus being diplontic while most algae are haplontic; red algae surviving at great depths.

Define heterospory with two examples; why bryophytes are amphibians; economic importance of algae (any two); coralloid roots and mycorrhiza; protonema versus prothallus; gemma cups; three classes of algae with one example each; ploidy questions from NCERT exercise 4; distinguish liverworts from mosses (two points).

Compare Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae on pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella; describe the life cycle of a moss or a fern with the site of meiosis; why gymnosperms and angiosperms are classified separately though both bear seeds; significance of heterospory; the three life-cycle patterns with one example each; economic importance of bryophytes and gymnosperms.

Important characteristics of gymnosperms with reproduction and a labelled diagram of Cycas or Pinus; the life cycle of a bryophyte (Funaria or Marchantia) with the alternation of generations drawn as a cycle; pteridophytes in full (features, heterospory, classes, life cycle); the three life-cycle patterns with annotated cycle diagrams and examples; a full account of algae with reproduction and importance.

A short passage on kelps or seaweeds followed by questions on pigments, reserve food, hydrocolloids and life cycle; a passage on Sphagnum and peat; a passage on Selaginella asking about heterospory and the seed habit; an unlabelled diagram of a moss, fern or Cycas to identify and comment on ploidy.

sections.heading: Introduction: how plants have been classified
sections.body:
In the previous chapter you met Whittaker's five kingdoms and saw that the cyanobacteria, once called blue-green algae, now sit in kingdom Monera, and that the fungi form their own kingdom. So when this chapter says plant kingdom it means only the true plants: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, taken in that order because that is the order in which they appeared in evolution and grew in complexity.

NCERT opens with a short history of classification systems, and a 1-mark or 2-mark question on it is common. Artificial systems were the earliest. Linnaeus's sexual system was of this kind: it used only a few vegetative characters or the structure of the androecium (stamens). The trouble is that such systems give equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters, and vegetative characters are easily changed by the environment, so unrelated plants get grouped together. Natural systems (Bentham and Hooker for flowering plants) were based on natural affinities and used a much wider set of features: external morphology and also internal features such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry. Phylogenetic systems, used today, arrange plants by evolutionary relationships, on the assumption that organisms in the same taxon share a common ancestor.

Three newer sources of evidence support phylogenetic classification. Numerical taxonomy uses computers: all observable characters are given numbers or codes, every character gets equal importance, and hundreds of characters are compared at once. Cytotaxonomy uses cytological information, chromosome number, structure and behaviour. Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of the plant. The examiner wants the pairing exact: Linnaeus and artificial, Bentham and Hooker and natural, chromosomes and cytotaxonomy, chemicals and chemotaxonomy, computers and numerical taxonomy.
sections.tip: Do not write that Linnaeus's system was 'wrong'. Write NCERT's reason: it separated closely related species because it relied on a few characters that the environment easily alters.

sections.heading: 3.1 Algae: general features, reproduction and importance
sections.body:
Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic organisms. Learn those five words in that order; they are the standard 1-mark definition. They live in fresh and marine water but also on moist stones, soils and wood, and some live in association with fungi (as lichens) and with animals (on the fur of the sloth bear). The body ranges from unicellular forms to colonies (Volvox), filaments (Ulothrix, Spirogyra) and the massive bodies of marine kelps.

Reproduction happens in three ways. Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation, each fragment growing into a thallus. Asexual reproduction is by spores, most commonly by zoospores, which are flagellated and motile and grow into new plants on release. Sexual reproduction is by fusion of gametes and is named by the gametes' size. Isogamy: the gametes are similar in size, either flagellated (Ulothrix) or non-flagellated (Spirogyra). Anisogamy: two gametes dissimilar in size, as in some species of Chlamydomonas. Oogamy: fusion between one large, non-motile female gamete and a smaller motile male gamete, as in Volvox and Fucus. The exemplar MCQ 'fusion of two motile gametes dissimilar in size' has the answer anisogamy.

Economic importance is a favourite 2-mark and 3-mark question. Algae carry out at least half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on earth by photosynthesis, and being photosynthetic they raise the level of dissolved oxygen in their surroundings. They are the primary producers of energy-rich compounds that form the basis of the food cycles of all aquatic animals. About 70 species of marine algae are used as food: Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum. Some marine brown and red algae produce hydrocolloids (water-holding substances): algin from brown algae and carrageen from red algae, both used commercially. Agar, from Gelidium and Gracilaria, is used to grow microbes and in the preparation of ice creams and jellies. Chlorella, a unicellular alga rich in proteins, is used as a food supplement even by space travellers. The old NCERT example of Spirulina is no longer in the text; Spirulina is a cyanobacterium, so stick to Chlorella.
sections.tip: Isogamy examples are the trap: Ulothrix (flagellated isogametes) and Spirogyra (non-flagellated isogametes). Oogamy: Volvox and Fucus. Anisogamy: some species of Chlamydomonas.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Chlorophyceae (green algae)
sections.body:
Members of Chlorophyceae are commonly called green algae. The plant body may be unicellular, colonial or filamentous. They are grass green because of the dominant pigments chlorophyll a and b, which are localised in definite chloroplasts. The chloroplasts may be discoid, plate-like, reticulate, cup-shaped, spiral or ribbon-shaped in different species; cup-shaped in Chlamydomonas and spiral (ribbon-shaped) in Spirogyra. Most members have one or more storage bodies called pyrenoids located in the chloroplasts. Pyrenoids contain protein besides starch. Some algae may store food as oil droplets. The cell wall has an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose.

Vegetative reproduction usually takes place by fragmentation or by the formation of different types of spores. Asexual reproduction is by flagellated zoospores produced in zoosporangia. Sexual reproduction shows considerable variation in the type and formation of sex cells and may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous. The flagella, when present, are 2 to 8, equal and apical (Table 3.1). Habitat: fresh water, brackish water and salt water.

Commonly found green algae you must be able to quote: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra and Chara. NCERT Figure 3.1 shows Chlamydomonas (unicellular, biflagellate, cup-shaped chloroplast with a pyrenoid, an eye spot and two contractile vacuoles), Volvox (a hollow spherical colony with daughter colonies inside) and Chara (a multicellular form with a stem-like axis and whorls of branches bearing the sex organs). A question that asks 'which alga has a cup-shaped chloroplast' or 'which is a colonial green alga' is testing this figure.
sections.tip: Pyrenoids store starch and protein; write both. 'Cellulose inside, pectose outside' is the wall answer for green algae; brown algae have cellulose with an algin coating.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Phaeophyceae (brown algae)
sections.body:
Brown algae are found primarily in marine habitats. They show great variation in size and form: from simple branched filamentous forms (Ectocarpus) to profusely branched forms represented by kelps, which may reach a height of 100 metres. They possess chlorophyll a, chlorophyll c, carotenoids and xanthophylls. Their colour varies from olive green to various shades of brown depending on the amount of the xanthophyll pigment fucoxanthin. Food is stored as complex carbohydrates, laminarin or mannitol (the exemplar asks for mannitol as the reserve food of brown algae). The vegetative cells have a cellulosic wall usually covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin. The protoplast contains plastids, a centrally located vacuole and a nucleus.

The plant body is usually attached to the substratum by a holdfast, and has a stalk, the stipe, and a leaf-like photosynthetic organ, the frond. This holdfast-stipe-frond organisation is a standard MCQ (answer: Phaeophyceae) and a standard diagram (NCERT Figure 3.2, Laminaria, Fucus, Dictyota).

Vegetative reproduction takes place by fragmentation. Asexual reproduction in most brown algae is by biflagellate zoospores that are pear-shaped and have two unequal, laterally attached flagella. Sexual reproduction may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous. Union of gametes may take place in water or within the oogonium (oogamous species). The gametes are pyriform (pear-shaped) and bear two laterally attached flagella. Habitat: fresh water (rare), brackish water and salt water. Common forms: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum and Fucus. Note two life-cycle facts used later: Fucus is diplontic and oogamous, while Ectocarpus and kelps are haplo-diplontic.
sections.tip: Flagella in brown algae: two, unequal, lateral. Green algae: two to eight, equal, apical. Red algae: none. This one row of Table 3.1 is asked more than any other.

sections.heading: 3.1.3 Rhodophyceae (red algae)
sections.body:
Members of Rhodophyceae are commonly called red algae because of the predominance of the red pigment r-phycoerythrin in their body. They possess chlorophyll a and d along with it (Table 3.1). Majority of red algae are marine, with a greater concentration in the warmer areas. They occur in both well-lighted regions close to the surface of water and also at great depths in oceans where relatively little light penetrates. Phycoerythrin absorbs the blue-green light that reaches deep water, which is the reasoning behind an Assertion–Reason item on red algae at depth. The red thalli of most red algae are multicellular, and some of them have complex body organisation.

The food is stored as floridean starch, which is very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure. The cell wall is of cellulose. Red algae usually reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation. They reproduce asexually by non-motile spores and sexually by non-motile gametes. Sexual reproduction is oogamous and is accompanied by complex post-fertilisation developments. Flagella are absent altogether, which is why the spores and gametes are non-motile. Habitat: fresh water (some), brackish water and salt water (most).

Common members: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria and Gelidium. Tie the names to uses: Porphyra is eaten, Gelidium and Gracilaria give agar, and carrageen is a red-algal hydrocolloid. Polysiphonia is the NCERT example of a haplo-diplontic alga along with Ectocarpus and kelps.

Table 3.1, which you should be able to reproduce from memory, reads: Chlorophyceae: chlorophyll a and b; starch; cellulose; flagella 2–8, equal, apical; fresh, brackish and salt water. Phaeophyceae: chlorophyll a and c, fucoxanthin; mannitol, laminarin; cellulose and algin; flagella 2, unequal, lateral; fresh water (rare), brackish, salt water. Rhodophyceae: chlorophyll a and d, phycoerythrin; floridean starch; cellulose; flagella absent; fresh water (some), brackish, salt water (most).
sections.tip: Red algae: everything non-motile. If an option says 'motile spores' or 'flagellated gametes' for Rhodophyceae it is wrong.

sections.heading: 3.2 Bryophytes: general features and importance
sections.body:
Bryophytes include the various mosses and liverworts that are found commonly growing in moist shaded areas in the hills. They are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because these plants can live in soil but are dependent on water for sexual reproduction; the antherozoids must swim to the archegonium. This single sentence is the most frequently asked 1-mark and 2-mark item in the chapter. They usually occur in damp, humid and shaded localities and play an important role in plant succession on bare rocks and soil.

The plant body is more differentiated than that of algae. It is thallus-like and prostrate or erect, attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids. Bryophytes lack true roots, stem or leaves; they may possess root-like, leaf-like or stem-like structures. The main plant body is haploid. It produces gametes, hence is called a gametophyte. The sex organs are multicellular (a contrast with algae). The male sex organ, the antheridium, produces biflagellate antherozoids. The female sex organ, the archegonium, is flask-shaped and produces a single egg. The antherozoids are released into water where they come in contact with the archegonium. An antherozoid fuses with the egg to produce the zygote. The zygote does not undergo reduction division immediately; it produces a multicellular body called a sporophyte. The sporophyte is not free-living but attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it. Some cells of the sporophyte undergo reduction division (meiosis) to produce haploid spores, which germinate to produce the gametophyte. So in a bryophyte meiosis happens in the capsule of the sporophyte, at spore formation.

Economic importance: bryophytes are of little economic importance in general, but some mosses provide food for herbaceous mammals, birds and other animals. Species of Sphagnum, a moss, provide peat, which has long been used as fuel, and because of its capacity to hold water it is used as packing material for trans-shipment of living material. Mosses along with lichens are the first organisms to colonise rocks; they decompose rocks, making the substrate suitable for the growth of higher plants. Since mosses form dense mats on the soil, they reduce the impact of falling rain and prevent soil erosion.
sections.tip: When asked why bryophytes are amphibians, give both halves: they live on land, and they need water for the biflagellate antherozoids to swim to the archegonium. One half earns one mark.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Liverworts
sections.body:
Liverworts grow usually in moist, shady habitats such as banks of streams, marshy ground, damp soil, bark of trees and deep in the woods. The plant body of a liverwort is thalloid, for example Marchantia. The thallus is dorsiventral (an upper and a lower surface that differ) and closely appressed to the substrate. The leafy members have tiny leaf-like appendages in two rows on the stem-like structures.

Asexual reproduction in liverworts takes place by fragmentation of thalli, or by the formation of specialised structures called gemmae (singular gemma). Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds which develop in small receptacles called gemma cups located on the thalli. The gemmae become detached from the parent body and germinate to form new individuals. Because a gemma is a piece of the gametophyte, a gemma cell is haploid (n), which is one of the ploidy items in NCERT exercise 4.

Sexual reproduction: the male and female sex organs are produced either on the same or on different thalli. In Marchantia they are carried on upright stalked structures, the antheridiophore and archegoniophore, which NCERT Figure 3.3 shows and which are useful labels in a diagram. The sporophyte is differentiated into a foot, seta and capsule. After meiosis, spores are produced within the capsule. These spores germinate to form free-living gametophytes. The examiner wants you to use the exact NCERT triplet foot, seta, capsule for the liverwort sporophyte, the same three parts as in mosses.
sections.tip: Gemmae are asexual, multicellular and haploid; they are not spores. 'Gemma cup' is the receptacle, 'gemma' is the bud.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Mosses
sections.body:
The predominant stage of the life cycle of a moss is the gametophyte, which consists of two stages. The first stage is the protonema: it develops directly from a spore and is a creeping, green, branched and frequently filamentous stage. Its ploidy is n; the exemplar MCQ 'protonema is haploid and found in mosses' tests exactly this, and the exercise asks for the ploidy of a protonemal cell (n). The second stage is the leafy stage, which develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud. It consists of upright, slender axes bearing spirally arranged leaves. The leafy stage is attached to the soil through multicellular and branched rhizoids and bears the sex organs. A leaf cell of a moss is therefore also haploid.

Vegetative reproduction in mosses is by fragmentation and budding in the secondary protonema. In sexual reproduction, the sex organs antheridia and archegonia are produced at the apex of the leafy shoots. After fertilisation the zygote develops into a sporophyte consisting of a foot, seta and capsule. The sporophyte in mosses is more elaborate than that in liverworts. The capsule contains spores, which are formed after meiosis. Mosses have an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal (the peristome teeth of the capsule, though NCERT does not name them). Common examples are Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum. NCERT Figure 3.3 shows Funaria as a leafy gametophyte with an attached sporophyte, plus Sphagnum and Polytrichum.

Liverworts versus mosses is a standard 2-mark or 3-mark question (NCERT exercise 9). Points: the liverwort gametophyte is thalloid and dorsiventral, the moss gametophyte has a protonema stage and a leafy stage with spirally arranged leaves; liverwort rhizoids are unicellular, moss rhizoids are multicellular and branched; liverworts reproduce asexually by gemmae, mosses by fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema; the moss sporophyte is more elaborate than the liverwort sporophyte and has an elaborate spore-dispersal mechanism. Examples: Marchantia versus Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum.
sections.tip: Protonema comes from the spore; the leafy stage comes from a lateral bud on the secondary protonema. Both are haploid gametophyte. The only diploid part of a moss is the sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) before meiosis.

sections.heading: 3.3 Pteridophytes: features, life cycle and heterospory
sections.body:
Pteridophytes include horsetails and ferns. They are used for medicinal purposes and as soil-binders, and are frequently grown as ornamentals. Evolutionarily they are the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues, xylem and phloem. They are found in cool, damp, shady places, though some flourish in sandy-soil conditions.

In pteridophytes the main plant body is a sporophyte, differentiated into true root, stem and leaves, with well-differentiated vascular tissues. The leaves may be small (microphylls) as in Selaginella or large (macrophylls) as in ferns. The sporophytes bear sporangia that are subtended by leaf-like appendages called sporophylls. In some cases the sporophylls form distinct compact structures called strobili or cones (Selaginella, Equisetum). The sporangia produce spores by meiosis in spore mother cells; this is the site of reduction division in a fern. The spores germinate to give rise to inconspicuous, small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophytes called prothallus. These gametophytes require cool, damp, shady places to grow, and because of this specific restricted requirement and the need for water for fertilisation, the spread of living pteridophytes is limited and restricted to narrow geographical regions. The gametophytes bear male and female sex organs, antheridia and archegonia. Water is required for the transfer of antherozoids, the male gametes released from the antheridia, to the mouth of the archegonium. Fusion of the male gamete with the egg produces a zygote, which develops into a multicellular well-differentiated sporophyte, the dominant phase. The prothallus is haploid, free-living and short-lived; the zygote of a fern is diploid.

Homospory and heterospory. In the majority of pteridophytes all the spores are of similar kind; such plants are homosporous (ferns such as Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum, and Equisetum). Genera like Selaginella and Salvinia produce two kinds of spores, macro (large) and micro (small), and are heterosporous. The megaspores and microspores germinate and give rise to female and male gametophytes respectively. In Selaginella and Salvinia the female gametophytes are retained on the parent sporophyte for variable periods, and the development of the zygote into a young embryo takes place within the female gametophyte. This event is a precursor to the seed habit, considered an important step in evolution. This is the significance of heterospory that the exercise question wants: two kinds of spores, two kinds of gametophyte, retention of the female gametophyte and embryo on the parent, hence the beginning of the seed habit. The exemplar asks why Selaginella still does not form a true seed: the female gametophyte is retained only for a while and there is no integument around the megasporangium and no protective seed coat, so the embryo is not released as a dormant seed.

Classes. Pteridophytes are further classified into four classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum); Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium); Sphenopsida (Equisetum); and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum). NCERT Figure 3.4 shows Selaginella, Equisetum and a fern; the fern sporophyte with a rhizome, fronds and sori on the underside of the leaflets is the diagram most often asked.
sections.tip: Prothallus = fern gametophyte (haploid, free-living, heart-shaped). Protonema = moss gametophyte stage. Students swap them; the examiner deducts.

sections.heading: 3.4 Gymnosperms
sections.body:
The name comes from gymnos, naked, and sperma, seed. In gymnosperms the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed, both before and after fertilisation. The seeds that develop after fertilisation are not covered, that is, they are naked. This is the whole answer to exercise 6 (why gymnosperms and angiosperms are classified separately though both bear seeds): in angiosperms the ovules are enclosed in the ovary and the seeds are enclosed in fruits.

Vegetative features. Gymnosperms include medium-sized trees or tall trees and shrubs. One of the gymnosperms, the giant redwood tree Sequoia, is one of the tallest tree species (the exemplar MCQ on the giant redwood expects gymnosperm). The roots are generally tap roots. Roots in some genera have fungal association in the form of mycorrhiza (Pinus), while in some others (Cycas) small specialised roots called coralloid roots are associated with N2-fixing cyanobacteria. The stems are unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). The leaves may be simple or compound. In Cycas the pinnate leaves persist for a few years. The leaves in gymnosperms are well adapted to withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. In conifers the needle-like leaves reduce the surface area; their thick cuticle and sunken stomata help to reduce water loss. Any 'adaptations of gymnosperm leaves' question wants these three phrases.

Reproduction. Gymnosperms are heterosporous: they produce haploid microspores and megaspores. The two kinds of spores are produced within sporangia borne on sporophylls which are arranged spirally along an axis to form lax or compact strobili or cones. The strobili bearing microsporophylls and microsporangia are called microsporangiate or male strobili. The microspores develop into a male gametophytic generation which is highly reduced and confined to only a limited number of cells; this reduced gametophyte is called a pollen grain, and its development takes place within the microsporangia. The cones bearing megasporophylls with ovules or megasporangia are called macrosporangiate or female strobili. The male and female cones may be borne on the same tree (Pinus) or on different trees (Cycas).

The megaspore mother cell is differentiated from one of the cells of the nucellus. The nucellus is protected by envelopes, and the composite structure is called an ovule. The ovules are borne on megasporophylls, which may be clustered to form the female cones. The megaspore mother cell divides meiotically to form four megaspores. One of the megaspores enclosed within the megasporangium develops into a multicellular female gametophyte that bears two or more archegonia. The multicellular female gametophyte is also retained within the megasporangium. Unlike bryophytes and pteridophytes, in gymnosperms the male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence; they remain within the sporangia retained on the sporophytes. The pollen grain is released from the microsporangium, carried in air currents, and comes in contact with the opening of the ovules borne on megasporophylls. The pollen tube carrying the male gametes grows towards the archegonia in the ovules and discharges its contents near the mouth of the archegonia. Following fertilisation the zygote develops into an embryo and the ovules into seeds; these seeds are not covered.

Gymnosperms are the third group (after bryophytes and pteridophytes) that bears archegonia; that is the answer to exercise 3. Economic importance (exercise 5): timber and soft wood from conifers, paper pulp from Pinus and other conifers, resin and turpentine from Pinus, edible seeds such as pine nuts (chilgoza) and the sago-like starch from the stem of Cycas, ephedrine from Ephedra, and ornamentals such as Cycas, Araucaria and Thuja.
sections.tip: Write 'ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall, exposed before and after fertilisation' word for word. 'Seeds without fruit' alone gets half marks.

sections.heading: 3.5 Angiosperms
sections.body:
In the rationalised NCERT this section is short: it defines the group and leaves the detail of the flower, gametophytes and double fertilisation to Class 12 (Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants). Unlike the gymnosperms where the ovules are naked, in angiosperms or flowering plants the pollen grains and ovules are developed in specialised structures called flowers, and the seeds are enclosed in fruits. The angiosperms are an exceptionally large group of plants occurring in a wide range of habitats. They range in size from the tiny, almost microscopic Wolffia to the tall trees of Eucalyptus (over 100 metres). They provide us with food, fodder, fuel, medicines and several other commercially important products.

They are divided into two classes: the dicotyledons and the monocotyledons. The dicotyledons are characterised by having two cotyledons in their seeds while the monocotyledons have only one. NCERT exercise 10 asks how you would distinguish monocots from dicots, and the school answer draws on what you already know from Class 9 and 10: dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate leaf venation, a tap-root system, tetramerous or pentamerous flowers and vascular bundles in a ring (open, with cambium); monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots, trimerous flowers and scattered closed vascular bundles.

Two facts from the old, now-deleted text still appear in school papers and in the NCERT exemplar, so keep them ready in one line each. The angiosperm embryo sac (female gametophyte) has 7 cells and 8 nuclei: an egg apparatus of one egg and two synergids at the micropylar end, three antipodals at the chalazal end, and a large central cell with two polar nuclei. Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms: one male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy, giving the diploid zygote) and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion, giving the triploid primary endosperm nucleus). If a plant has 2n = 36, its gametes have 18 and its endosperm has 3 × 18 = 54 chromosomes; that is the exemplar calculation. The primary endosperm nucleus in a dicot is 3n and the meristem cell of a monocot is 2n, the two ploidy items in exercise 4 that come from angiosperms.
sections.tip: Wolffia (smallest) and Eucalyptus over 100 m (tallest) are the NCERT size examples for angiosperms; Sequoia is the tall gymnosperm. Do not mix them.

sections.heading: 3.6 Plant Life Cycles and Alternation of Generations
sections.body:
In plants, both haploid and diploid cells can divide by mitosis. This property leads to the formation of different plant bodies, haploid and diploid. The haploid plant body produces gametes by mitosis; this plant body represents a gametophyte. Following fertilisation the zygote also divides by mitosis to produce a diploid sporophytic plant body. Haploid spores are produced by this plant body by meiosis. These in turn divide by mitosis to form a haploid plant body once again. Thus during the life cycle of any sexually reproducing plant there is an alternation of generations between the gamete-producing haploid gametophyte and the spore-producing diploid sporophyte. The three patterns differ only in which phase is dominant and free-living (NCERT Figure 3.7).

(a) Haplontic. The sporophytic generation is represented only by the one-celled zygote. There are no free-living sporophytes. Meiosis in the zygote results in the formation of haploid spores. The haploid spores divide mitotically and form the gametophyte. The dominant, photosynthetic phase is the free-living gametophyte. Examples: many algae such as Volvox, Spirogyra and some species of Chlamydomonas.

(b) Diplontic. The diploid sporophyte is the dominant, photosynthetic, independent phase. The gametophytic phase is represented by a single to few-celled haploid gametophyte. All seed-bearing plants, gymnosperms and angiosperms, follow this pattern with some variations, wherein the gametophytic phase is few to multi-celled. Among algae, Fucus is diplontic. Here meiosis happens at spore (gamete) formation in the sporophyte.

(c) Haplo-diplontic. This is the intermediate condition. Both phases are multicellular and often free-living; however, they differ in their dominant phases. In bryophytes a dominant, independent, photosynthetic, thalloid or erect gametophyte alternates with a short-lived multicellular sporophyte that is totally or partially dependent on the gametophyte for anchorage and nutrition. In pteridophytes the diploid sporophyte is the dominant, independent, photosynthetic, vascular plant body; it alternates with a multicellular, saprophytic or autotrophic, independent but short-lived haploid gametophyte. Interestingly, while most algal genera are haplontic, some such as Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps are haplo-diplontic.

Exercise 2 asks when and where reduction division takes place in five plants; the answer is one line each. Liverwort: in the capsule of the sporophyte, at spore formation. Moss: in the capsule of the sporophyte, at spore formation. Fern: in the spore mother cells inside the sporangia on the sporophylls (sori), at spore formation. Gymnosperm: in the microspore mother cells in the microsporangia (male cone) and in the megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule (female cone). Angiosperm: in the microspore mother cells of the anther and in the megaspore mother cell of the ovule inside the ovary. In every case meiosis happens at spore formation, never at gamete formation, because plant gametes are made by mitosis.
sections.tip: Fucus is the exception among algae (diplontic); Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps are the other exception (haplo-diplontic). The rest of the algae named in the chapter are haplontic.

key_terms.definition: A classification based on a few superficial characters, such as Linnaeus's sexual system using vegetative characters or the structure of the androecium; it gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters even though vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment.
A system based on evolutionary relationships, assuming that organisms placed in the same taxon share a common ancestor; supported by numerical taxonomy, cytotaxonomy and chemotaxonomy.
Cytotaxonomy uses cytological information (chromosome number, structure and behaviour) and chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of a plant to resolve classification problems.
Chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic (fresh water and marine) organisms, ranging from unicellular forms to colonies, filaments and massive kelps.

Isogamy is the fusion of two gametes similar in size (Ulothrix, Spirogyra); anisogamy the fusion of two gametes dissimilar in size (some species of Chlamydomonas); oogamy the fusion of one large non-motile female gamete with a smaller motile male gamete (Volvox, Fucus).
A flagellated, motile asexual spore produced in a zoosporangium, the commonest asexual spore of green and brown algae; on release it grows into a new plant.
A storage body located in the chloroplast of green algae that contains protein in addition to starch.
The xanthophyll pigment of Phaeophyceae whose amount decides the colour of a brown alga, from olive green to various shades of brown.
The reserve food of red algae (Rhodophyceae), very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure.
Water-holding substances produced by marine algae: algin from brown algae, carrageen from red algae, and agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria, used to grow microbes and in ice creams and jellies.
Bryophytes, because they can live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction, the biflagellate antherozoids swimming to the archegonium.
The multicellular sex organs of bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms: the antheridium (male) produces antherozoids, the flask-shaped archegonium (female) produces a single egg.
Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds of liverworts that develop in small receptacles called gemma cups on the thallus; they detach and germinate into new individuals.
The first stage of the moss gametophyte, developing directly from the spore: creeping, green, branched and frequently filamentous; the leafy stage arises from it as a lateral bud.
The gametophyte of a pteridophyte: an inconspicuous, small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid structure that bears antheridia and archegonia.

A sporophyll is a leaf-like appendage that subtends sporangia; sporangia produce spores by meiosis; in Selaginella, Equisetum and gymnosperms sporophylls are packed into compact structures called strobili or cones.

Homosporous plants produce one kind of spore (most ferns, Equisetum); heterosporous plants produce megaspores and microspores that grow into female and male gametophytes (Selaginella, Salvinia, all seed plants).

Retention of the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte and development of the zygote into an embryo within it, first seen in the heterosporous pteridophytes Selaginella and Salvinia, and considered a precursor to the seed.
Coralloid roots are small specialised roots of Cycas associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria; mycorrhiza is the fungal association of the roots of Pinus.
The highly reduced male gametophyte of gymnosperms and angiosperms, confined to a limited number of cells and developed within the microsporangium.
The composite structure formed by the nucellus (megasporangium), which contains the megaspore mother cell, protected by envelopes; naked in gymnosperms, enclosed in an ovary in angiosperms.

key_terms.term: Haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic life cycles
key_terms.definition: Haplontic: only the zygote is diploid, meiosis is zygotic (Volvox, Spirogyra). Diplontic: the sporophyte dominates and the gametophyte is one to a few cells (Fucus, gymnosperms, angiosperms). Haplo-diplontic: both phases multicellular and often free-living (bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps).

The alternation in a plant life cycle between a haploid gamete-producing gametophyte and a diploid spore-producing sporophyte, possible because in plants both haploid and diploid cells can divide by mitosis.

formula_sheet.name: Table 3.1 Chlorophyceae
formula_sheet.expr: Pigments chlorophyll a, b; stored food starch (in pyrenoids with protein); wall cellulose inside, pectose outside; flagella 2–8, equal, apical; fresh, brackish and salt water

formula_sheet.name: Table 3.1 Phaeophyceae
formula_sheet.expr: Pigments chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin; stored food mannitol, laminarin; wall cellulose with algin coating; flagella 2, unequal, lateral; fresh water rare, mostly marine
formula_sheet.note: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus; body = holdfast, stipe, frond; kelps up to 100 m

formula_sheet.name: Table 3.1 Rhodophyceae
formula_sheet.expr: Pigments chlorophyll a, d, r-phycoerythrin; stored food floridean starch; wall cellulose; flagella absent, spores and gametes non-motile, oogamous
formula_sheet.note: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium; found even at great depths

formula_sheet.name: Sexual reproduction in algae
formula_sheet.expr: Isogamy: Ulothrix (flagellated), Spirogyra (non-flagellated); anisogamy: some Chlamydomonas species; oogamy: Volvox, Fucus
formula_sheet.note: Named by the size of gametes, not by motility

formula_sheet.name: Economic importance of algae
formula_sheet.expr: At least half of earth's CO<sub>2</sub> fixation; ~70 marine species eaten (Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum); algin (brown), carrageen (red); agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria; Chlorella protein supplement for space travellers

formula_sheet.name: Bryophyte facts
formula_sheet.expr: Gametophyte dominant and haploid; unicellular or multicellular rhizoids; antheridium → biflagellate antherozoids; flask-shaped archegonium → one egg; sporophyte = foot, seta, capsule, dependent on gametophyte; meiosis in capsule
formula_sheet.note: Liverwort: Marchantia (thalloid, dorsiventral, gemma cups). Mosses: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum (protonema then leafy stage)

formula_sheet.name: Economic importance of bryophytes
formula_sheet.expr: Sphagnum → peat (fuel) and packing material for living material because it holds water; mosses + lichens pioneer bare rocks; moss mats prevent soil erosion; food for some mammals and birds

formula_sheet.name: Pteridophyte facts
formula_sheet.expr: First terrestrial plants with xylem and phloem; sporophyte dominant with true root, stem, leaves; microphylls (Selaginella) or macrophylls (ferns); gametophyte = free-living prothallus; meiosis in spore mother cells in sporangia
formula_sheet.note: Heterosporous: Selaginella, Salvinia. Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum)

formula_sheet.name: Gymnosperm facts
formula_sheet.expr: Naked ovules and seeds; tap roots; mycorrhiza (Pinus), coralloid roots with N<sub>2</sub>-fixing cyanobacteria (Cycas); needle leaves, thick cuticle, sunken stomata; heterosporous; male and female strobili on same tree (Pinus) or different trees (Cycas); gametophytes never free-living; wind-carried pollen, pollen tube to archegonia
formula_sheet.note: Sequoia (giant redwood) one of the tallest trees; Cycas pinnate leaves persist a few years; unbranched stem Cycas, branched Pinus and Cedrus

formula_sheet.name: Angiosperm facts
formula_sheet.expr: Pollen and ovules in flowers; seeds inside fruits; Wolffia (microscopic) to Eucalyptus (over 100 m); dicots two cotyledons, monocots one
formula_sheet.note: Embryo sac 7 cells 8 nuclei; endosperm 3n (for 2n = 36, endosperm = 54); these details are examined though moved to Class 12

formula_sheet.name: Ploidy list (NCERT exercise 4)
formula_sheet.expr: Protonemal cell of moss n; primary endosperm nucleus of dicot 3n; leaf cell of moss n; prothallus cell of fern n; gemma cell of Marchantia n; meristem cell of monocot 2n; ovum of liverwort n; zygote of fern 2n
formula_sheet.note: Gametophyte parts are always n, sporophyte parts 2n, endosperm 3n

formula_sheet.name: Life-cycle patterns
formula_sheet.expr: Haplontic (zygotic meiosis): Volvox, Spirogyra, some Chlamydomonas. Diplontic: Fucus, gymnosperms, angiosperms. Haplo-diplontic: bryophytes (gametophyte dominant), pteridophytes (sporophyte dominant), Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps
formula_sheet.note: Meiosis always makes spores; gametes are always made by mitosis in plants

formula_sheet.name: Site of reduction division (exercise 2)
formula_sheet.expr: Liverwort and moss: capsule of sporophyte; fern: spore mother cells in sporangia on sporophylls; gymnosperm: microspore mother cells in microsporangia of male cone and megaspore mother cell in nucellus of ovule; angiosperm: anther and ovule inside ovary

diagrams.title: Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Chara (NCERT Figure 3.1, green algae)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw Chlamydomonas as an oval cell with two equal apical flagella, a cup-shaped chloroplast filling most of the cell, one pyrenoid inside the chloroplast, a nucleus in the cup, an eye spot near the front and two contractile vacuoles at the anterior end; label cell wall, flagella, chloroplast, pyrenoid, nucleus, eye spot, contractile vacuole. Beside it draw Volvox as a large hollow sphere of small biflagellate cells with two or three daughter colonies inside, labelled. Draw Chara as an upright axis with nodes bearing whorls of short branches, labelled node, internode, branch, and the sex organs (globule and nucule) at a node. Caption each with its class, Chlorophyceae.

diagrams.title: Laminaria, Fucus and Dictyota (NCERT Figure 3.2, brown algae)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw Laminaria as a large flat blade attached to a rock by a branched root-like base; label holdfast (attachment), stipe (the stalk) and frond (the leaf-like photosynthetic blade). Draw Fucus as a flattened, repeatedly forked (dichotomous) thallus with a midrib and swollen tips; label the receptacles (swollen fertile tips), air bladders and holdfast. Draw Dictyota as a small flat dichotomously branched ribbon. Caption: Phaeophyceae, marine, pigments chlorophyll a, c and fucoxanthin, reserve food mannitol and laminarin.

diagrams.title: Marchantia gametophyte with gemma cups and sex organs (NCERT Figure 3.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a flat, dorsiventral, dichotomously branched thallus lying on the ground with a faint midrib and a notch at each growing tip. On the upper surface draw two or three small cups holding tiny green discs; label gemma cup and gemmae (asexual buds). From the underside draw fine hairs labelled rhizoids (unicellular) and scales. Draw one upright stalk ending in a lobed disc labelled antheridiophore (bears antheridia, male), and another ending in a star-shaped umbrella labelled archegoniophore (bears archegonia, female). Caption: liverwort, haploid gametophyte, thalloid.

diagrams.title: Funaria (moss) gametophyte with attached sporophyte (NCERT Figure 3.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a short upright stem with small spirally arranged leaves, anchored below by branched multicellular rhizoids; label leafy gametophyte, leaves, rhizoids. From the tip draw a long slender stalk carrying a swollen pear-shaped capsule at the top; label foot (embedded in the gametophyte tip), seta and capsule, and draw a small cap on the capsule labelled calyptra with the operculum below it. Mark ploidy on the drawing: gametophyte n, sporophyte 2n, spores in the capsule n after meiosis. Caption: sporophyte dependent on the gametophyte, haplo-diplontic.

diagrams.title: Antheridium and archegonium of a bryophyte
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the antheridium as a club-shaped body on a short stalk with a single-layered sterile jacket enclosing many small cells; label stalk, jacket layer and androcytes (antherozoid mother cells), with a free biflagellate antherozoid drawn beside it. Draw the archegonium as a flask: a swollen base (venter) enclosing one large egg cell and a ventral canal cell, and a long neck with neck canal cells and a ring of cover cells at the mouth; label venter, egg, ventral canal cell, neck, neck canal cells, cover cells. Caption: multicellular sex organs; antherozoids need water to reach the archegonium.

diagrams.title: Fern (Dryopteris) sporophyte with sorus, and the prothallus (NCERT Figure 3.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal underground rhizome with adventitious roots below and two or three large pinnately compound leaves (fronds) rising from it, one with a coiled young tip labelled circinate vernation. On the underside of one leaflet draw small dots labelled sori; enlarge one sorus to show a group of stalked sporangia under a flap labelled indusium, with one sporangium showing its annulus and spores. Below draw the prothallus as a small heart-shaped green plate with rhizoids, archegonia near the notch and antheridia among the rhizoids; label all and write prothallus, haploid, free-living gametophyte. Caption: sporophyte dominant, meiosis in the sporangia.

diagrams.title: Selaginella and Equisetum (NCERT Figure 3.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw Selaginella as a creeping branched stem covered with small microphylls in four rows, with root-bearing rhizophores from the branch points and a compact terminal cone; label microphylls, rhizophore, strobilus (cone), and in a cut cone label megasporophyll with megasporangium and microsporophyll with microsporangium to show heterospory. Draw Equisetum as a jointed hollow upright stem with whorls of small scale leaves and branches at each node, a rhizome below and a terminal cone; label node, internode, whorl of scale leaves, strobilus. Caption: Lycopsida (heterosporous) and Sphenopsida (homosporous).

diagrams.title: Cycas and Pinus (NCERT Figure 3.5, gymnosperms)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw Cycas as a stout unbranched columnar trunk covered with persistent leaf bases and a crown of large pinnate leaves at the top; label trunk (unbranched), pinnate leaves, and at the base draw a cluster of short, dichotomously branched roots labelled coralloid roots (with N2-fixing cyanobacteria). Draw a separate male cone and a loose female cone (megasporophylls with exposed ovules) and write that they are on different trees. Draw Pinus as a branched tree with needle-shaped leaves in bundles; label branched stem, needle leaves, male cone (cluster of microsporangiate strobili) and female cone (woody, with exposed ovules on cone scales), and write both cones on the same tree, roots with mycorrhiza. Caption: ovules naked.

diagrams.title: The three life-cycle patterns (NCERT Figure 3.7)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three circles. In each, mark a haploid arc (n, gametophyte) and a diploid arc (2n, sporophyte), with the arrow gametes → zygote labelled fertilisation and the arrow sporophyte → spores labelled meiosis (R!). Haplontic: draw the diploid arc as a single dot labelled zygote, with meiosis right after it, and write Volvox, Spirogyra. Diplontic: draw the haploid arc as a tiny segment labelled few-celled gametophyte and the diploid arc as the whole circle, and write Fucus, gymnosperms, angiosperms. Haplo-diplontic: draw both arcs long, and write bryophytes (gametophyte dominant), pteridophytes (sporophyte dominant), Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps. Caption: gametes by mitosis, spores by meiosis.

ncert_questions.q: What is the basis of classification of algae?
ncert_questions.a: Algae are classified mainly on the basis of (i) the pigments present in the cell, (ii) the nature of the stored food, (iii) the composition of the cell wall, and (iv) the number, position and type of flagella. On these grounds they fall into three classes: Chlorophyceae (chlorophyll a and b, starch, cellulose and pectose wall, 2–8 equal apical flagella; Spirogyra, Chara), Phaeophyceae (chlorophyll a and c with fucoxanthin, mannitol and laminarin, cellulose with algin, two unequal lateral flagella; Laminaria, Fucus) and Rhodophyceae (chlorophyll a and d with r-phycoerythrin, floridean starch, cellulose, flagella absent; Porphyra, Polysiphonia).

ncert_questions.q: When and where does reduction division take place in the life cycle of a liverwort, a moss, a fern, a gymnosperm and an angiosperm?
ncert_questions.a:
In every case reduction division (meiosis) takes place at the time of spore formation in the sporophyte; the site differs.

  • Liverwort: in the spore mother cells inside the capsule of the sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule), producing haploid spores.
  • Moss: in the spore mother cells inside the capsule of the sporophyte borne on the leafy gametophyte.
  • Fern: in the spore mother cells inside the sporangia, which are grouped as sori on the underside of the sporophylls (leaves).
  • Gymnosperm: in the microspore mother cells in the microsporangia of the male cone (forming microspores that become pollen grains) and in the megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule on the megasporophyll of the female cone (forming four megaspores).
  • Angiosperm: in the microspore mother cells in the pollen sacs of the anther and in the megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule inside the ovary of the flower.

ncert_questions.q: Name three groups of plants that bear archegonia. Briefly describe the life cycle of any one of them.
ncert_questions.a:
Archegonia are borne by bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms.

Life cycle of a moss (bryophyte): The dominant plant body is the haploid gametophyte. A spore germinates into the protonema, a creeping green filamentous stage, from which the leafy stage arises as a lateral bud; the leafy shoot is anchored by multicellular branched rhizoids. Antheridia and archegonia develop at the apex of the leafy shoots. The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids that swim in water to the flask-shaped archegonium and fuse with its single egg to form a diploid zygote. The zygote does not undergo meiosis; it divides mitotically into a sporophyte differentiated into foot, seta and capsule, which stays attached to the gametophyte and draws nourishment from it. Spore mother cells in the capsule undergo meiosis to produce haploid spores, which are dispersed and germinate to form the protonema again. Thus a multicellular gametophyte alternates with a dependent multicellular sporophyte: the haplo-diplontic pattern with the gametophyte dominant.

ncert_questions.q: Mention the ploidy of the following: protonemal cell of a moss; primary endosperm nucleus in a dicot; leaf cell of a moss; prothallus cell of a fern; gemma cell in Marchantia; meristem cell of a monocot; ovum of a liverwort; zygote of a fern.
ncert_questions.a:
• Protonemal cell of a moss: haploid (n), part of the gametophyte.
  • Primary endosperm nucleus in a dicot: triploid (3n), formed by triple fusion of one male gamete with two polar nuclei.
  • Leaf cell of a moss: haploid (n).
  • Prothallus cell of a fern: haploid (n).
  • Gemma cell in Marchantia: haploid (n), gemmae are asexual buds of the gametophyte.
  • Meristem cell of a monocot: diploid (2n), part of the sporophyte plant.
  • Ovum of a liverwort: haploid (n), a gamete.
  • Zygote of a fern: diploid (2n), product of fertilisation.

ncert_questions.q: Write a note on the economic importance of algae and gymnosperms.
ncert_questions.a:
Algae: (i) They carry out at least half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on earth by photosynthesis and, being photosynthetic, increase the dissolved oxygen in their surroundings. (ii) They are the primary producers of energy-rich compounds that form the basis of the food cycles of all aquatic animals. (iii) About 70 species of marine algae are used as food, for example Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum. (iv) Brown and red algae yield hydrocolloids: algin from brown algae and carrageen from red algae, used commercially. (v) Agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria is used to grow microbes and in ice creams and jellies. (vi) Chlorella, a unicellular alga rich in protein, is used as a food supplement even by space travellers.

Gymnosperms: (i) Conifers such as Pinus, Cedrus and Sequoia give timber and soft wood used in construction and furniture. (ii) Wood pulp of conifers is used for paper. (iii) Resin, turpentine and Canada balsam are obtained from conifers; ephedrine, used in respiratory disorders, from Ephedra. (iv) Seeds of Pinus gerardiana (chilgoza) are eaten, and sago is prepared from the stem of Cycas. (v) Cycas, Thuja, Araucaria and Ginkgo are grown as ornamentals.

ncert_questions.q: Both gymnosperms and angiosperms bear seeds, then why are they classified separately?
ncert_questions.a: Because the ovules and seeds are placed differently. In gymnosperms the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall; they remain exposed on the megasporophylls both before and after fertilisation, so the seeds are naked, borne on cone scales, and no fruit is formed. In angiosperms the ovules are enclosed within the ovary of a flower, pollen grains and ovules develop in flowers, and after fertilisation the ovary ripens into a fruit that encloses the seeds. Gymnosperms also lack double fertilisation and true vessels (mostly), and their pollination is by wind onto the ovule directly, while angiosperm pollen lands on a stigma. Hence the two seed-bearing groups are classified separately.

ncert_questions.q: What is heterospory? Briefly comment on its significance. Give two examples.
ncert_questions.a:
Heterospory is the production of two different kinds of spores by a sporophyte: large megaspores (macrospores) in megasporangia and small microspores in microsporangia. The megaspore germinates into the female gametophyte and the microspore into the male gametophyte.

Significance: In heterosporous pteridophytes the female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte for a variable period, and the zygote develops into a young embryo inside the female gametophyte, which protects and nourishes it. This retention of the female gametophyte and embryo on the parent plant is the precursor to the seed habit, an important step in evolution that led to the seed plants.

Examples: Selaginella and Salvinia among pteridophytes (all gymnosperms and angiosperms are also heterosporous).

ncert_questions.q: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples: (i) protonema (ii) antheridium (iii) archegonium (iv) diplontic (v) sporophyll (vi) isogamy.
ncert_questions.a:
• Protonema: the first stage of the gametophyte of a moss, developing directly from the spore; it is creeping, green, branched and frequently filamentous, and gives rise to the leafy stage as a lateral bud. Example: Funaria.
  • Antheridium: the multicellular male sex organ of bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms; a jacketed body that produces antherozoids (biflagellate in bryophytes). Example: Marchantia, fern prothallus.
  • Archegonium: the multicellular flask-shaped female sex organ with a neck and a venter that produces a single egg. Example: Funaria, Dryopteris, Pinus.
  • Diplontic: a life cycle in which the diploid sporophyte is the dominant, photosynthetic, independent phase and the gametophyte is reduced to a single to few cells. Example: Fucus, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
  • Sporophyll: a leaf-like appendage that bears sporangia; in Selaginella and Equisetum sporophylls are packed into strobili (cones), and in gymnosperms microsporophylls and megasporophylls form male and female cones. Example: fern leaf bearing sori.
  • Isogamy: sexual reproduction by fusion of two gametes similar in size, either flagellated (Ulothrix) or non-flagellated (Spirogyra).

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between the following: (i) red algae and brown algae (ii) liverworts and moss (iii) homosporous and heterosporous pteridophyte (iv) syngamy and triple fusion.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Red algae vs brown algae: Red algae (Rhodophyceae) have chlorophyll a, d and r-phycoerythrin, store floridean starch, have a cellulose wall, lack flagella so their spores and gametes are non-motile, and occur even at great depths; examples Porphyra, Polysiphonia. Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) have chlorophyll a, c and fucoxanthin, store mannitol and laminarin, have a cellulose wall coated with algin, produce biflagellate pear-shaped zoospores and gametes with two unequal lateral flagella, and have a holdfast, stipe and frond; examples Laminaria, Fucus.

(ii) Liverworts vs moss: Liverworts have a thalloid, dorsiventral gametophyte with unicellular rhizoids, reproduce asexually by gemmae in gemma cups, and have a simple sporophyte; example Marchantia. Mosses have a gametophyte in two stages, a filamentous protonema and a leafy stage with spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids, reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema, and have a more elaborate sporophyte with a spore-dispersal mechanism; examples Funaria, Sphagnum.

(iii) Homosporous vs heterosporous pteridophyte: A homosporous pteridophyte produces only one kind of spore, which grows into a bisexual prothallus bearing both antheridia and archegonia; examples Dryopteris, Equisetum. A heterosporous pteridophyte produces megaspores and microspores that grow into separate female and male gametophytes, the female gametophyte being retained on the parent plant; examples Selaginella, Salvinia.

(iv) Syngamy vs triple fusion: Syngamy is the fusion of one male gamete with the egg cell to form the diploid (2n) zygote. Triple fusion is the fusion of the second male gamete with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus. Both together make up double fertilisation in angiosperms.

ncert_questions.q: How would you distinguish monocots from dicots?
ncert_questions.a: Monocots have one cotyledon in the seed, dicots have two. Monocot leaves show parallel venation, dicot leaves reticulate venation. Monocots have a fibrous (adventitious) root system, dicots a tap-root system. Monocot flowers are trimerous (parts in threes), dicot flowers tetramerous or pentamerous. Monocot stems have scattered, closed vascular bundles without cambium, so no secondary growth; dicot stems have vascular bundles in a ring, open with cambium, so secondary growth occurs. Examples: wheat, maize, lily (monocots); pea, mustard, sunflower (dicots).

ncert_questions.q: Match the following (column I with column II): (a) Chlamydomonas (b) Cycas (c) Selaginella (d) Sphagnum with (i) Moss (ii) Pteridophyte (iii) Algae (iv) Gymnosperm.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Chlamydomonas – (iii) Algae (a unicellular green alga, Chlorophyceae).
(b) Cycas – (iv) Gymnosperm (naked ovules, coralloid roots).
(c) Selaginella – (ii) Pteridophyte (heterosporous, Lycopsida).
(d) Sphagnum – (i) Moss (peat moss, Bryophyta).

ncert_questions.q: Describe the important characteristics of gymnosperms.
ncert_questions.a:
1. Gymnosperms (gymnos: naked, sperma: seed) are plants in which the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed before and after fertilisation, so the seeds are naked, not enclosed in a fruit.
2. They are medium-sized to tall trees and shrubs; Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest tree species.
3. Roots are generally tap roots; in Pinus the roots have a fungal association (mycorrhiza), and in Cycas small specialised coralloid roots harbour nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
4. Stems are unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). Leaves are simple or compound; the pinnate leaves of Cycas persist for a few years. Leaves are adapted to extremes of temperature, humidity and wind: conifers have needle-like leaves that reduce surface area, with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata that reduce water loss.
5. They are heterosporous, producing microspores and megaspores in sporangia borne on sporophylls arranged spirally into strobili or cones. Male (microsporangiate) and female (megasporangiate) cones occur on the same tree (Pinus) or on different trees (Cycas).
6. The male gametophyte is reduced to the pollen grain, formed within the microsporangium. The megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule divides by meiosis; one megaspore forms a multicellular female gametophyte bearing two or more archegonia, retained within the megasporangium. Neither gametophyte is free-living.
7. Pollen grains are carried by wind to the opening of the ovule; a pollen tube carries the male gametes to the archegonia. After fertilisation the zygote forms an embryo and the ovule becomes a naked seed. The life cycle is diplontic with the sporophyte dominant.

ncert_questions.q: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
ncert_questions.a: Bryophytes such as mosses and liverworts live on land, in moist and shaded places, but they cannot complete their life cycle without water. The male gametes, the biflagellate antherozoids released from the antheridium, must swim through a film of water to reach the archegonium and fertilise the egg. Because they live in soil yet depend on water for sexual reproduction, like amphibians they lead a double life, and are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

ncert_questions.q: Selaginella shows heterospory and the beginning of the seed habit, yet it does not form true seeds. Why?
ncert_questions.a: Selaginella is heterosporous and retains the female gametophyte with the developing embryo on the parent sporophyte, which is the first step towards the seed habit. But it does not form a true seed because (i) the megasporangium is not covered by integuments, so no seed coat forms; (ii) the female gametophyte is retained only for a variable period and the megaspore is eventually shed, so the embryo does not develop fully on the parent plant; (iii) there is no period of dormancy and no stored food reserve of the kind a seed has; and (iv) it still needs water for the motile antherozoids to reach the archegonia. A true seed requires an integumented, permanently retained megasporangium in which the embryo matures and then rests.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the haplo-diplontic life cycle with the help of a labelled diagram, and explain how the two dominant phases differ in bryophytes and pteridophytes.
ncert_questions.a:
In a haplo-diplontic life cycle both the haploid gametophyte and the diploid sporophyte are multicellular and often free-living, and the two alternate regularly. Draw a circle: the haploid gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis in antheridia and archegonia; gametes fuse (fertilisation) to form the diploid zygote; the zygote divides by mitosis into a multicellular sporophyte; spore mother cells in the sporophyte undergo meiosis to form haploid spores; spores divide mitotically to form the gametophyte again. Label fertilisation and meiosis as the two points where ploidy changes.

In bryophytes the gametophyte is the dominant phase: an independent, photosynthetic, thalloid or erect plant body (Marchantia thallus, Funaria leafy shoot). The sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) is short-lived, multicellular and totally or partially dependent on the gametophyte for anchorage and nutrition. In pteridophytes the sporophyte is the dominant phase: an independent, photosynthetic, vascular plant with true roots, stem and leaves (the fern plant). The gametophyte, the prothallus, is multicellular, independent and photosynthetic (or saprophytic) but small and short-lived. Some algae, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps, are also haplo-diplontic.

pyq.answer: c

pyq.answer: c

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
