pyq.q: Name the three classes of algae and give one example of each.
pyq.answer: Chlorophyceae (green algae): Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra or Chara. Phaeophyceae (brown algae): Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum or Fucus. Rhodophyceae (red algae): Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria or Gelidium. (Half mark for each class name, half for each example.)

pyq.q: What are gemmae? Where are they formed and what is their function?
pyq.answer: Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds of liverworts such as Marchantia. They develop inside small receptacles called gemma cups located on the upper surface of the thallus. They become detached from the parent body and germinate to form new individuals, so they are a means of asexual (vegetative) reproduction. Being part of the gametophyte, gemma cells are haploid.

pyq.q: Mention two adaptations in the leaves of conifers that help them withstand extreme conditions.
pyq.answer: (i) The leaves are needle-like, which reduces the surface area exposed to wind, heat and cold. (ii) The leaves have a thick cuticle and sunken stomata, which reduce water loss by transpiration. Together these let gymnosperms withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind.

pyq.q: Distinguish between protonema and prothallus.
pyq.answer: Protonema is the first stage of the gametophyte of a moss: it develops directly from the spore and is a creeping, green, branched, frequently filamentous structure from which the leafy stage arises as a lateral bud. Prothallus is the entire gametophyte of a pteridophyte (fern): a small, heart-shaped, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid body that develops from the spore and bears antheridia and archegonia. Both are haploid.

pyq.q: Give two points of economic importance of bryophytes.
pyq.answer: (i) Species of Sphagnum provide peat, which is used as fuel, and because of its water-holding capacity Sphagnum is used as packing material for trans-shipment of living material. (ii) Mosses along with lichens are the first organisms to colonise bare rocks; they decompose the rock and make the substrate suitable for higher plants. (Also acceptable: moss mats reduce the impact of falling rain and prevent soil erosion; some mosses are food for herbaceous mammals and birds.)

pyq.q: Compare Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae with respect to major pigments, stored food and flagella.
pyq.answer:
Chlorophyceae: pigments chlorophyll a and b (grass green); stored food starch, in pyrenoids that also contain protein; flagella 2 to 8, equal, apical.
Phaeophyceae: pigments chlorophyll a and c with the xanthophyll fucoxanthin (olive green to brown); stored food mannitol and laminarin; flagella two, unequal, laterally attached.
Rhodophyceae: pigments chlorophyll a and d with r-phycoerythrin (red); stored food floridean starch, similar to amylopectin and glycogen; flagella absent, so spores and gametes are non-motile.
Cell wall for completeness: cellulose and pectose (green), cellulose with algin (brown), cellulose (red).

pyq.q: Describe the life cycle of a fern, mentioning the ploidy of each stage and the point of meiosis.
pyq.answer: The fern plant seen in nature is the diploid sporophyte (2n), differentiated into a rhizome (stem), adventitious roots and large leaves (fronds). On the underside of the fronds, sporangia are grouped into sori. Spore mother cells (2n) inside the sporangia undergo meiosis to produce haploid spores (n); this is the only point of reduction division. A spore germinates into the prothallus, a small heart-shaped, free-living, photosynthetic gametophyte (n) bearing antheridia and archegonia on its lower surface. Antheridia release flagellated antherozoids (n) that swim in water to the archegonium and fuse with the egg (n), forming a diploid zygote (2n). The zygote divides by mitosis into an embryo and then a new sporophyte, which soon becomes independent while the prothallus withers. The cycle is haplo-diplontic with the sporophyte dominant.

pyq.q: Explain the three patterns of plant life cycle, giving one example of each.
pyq.answer:
Haplontic: the haploid gametophyte is the dominant, photosynthetic, free-living phase; the sporophyte is represented only by the one-celled zygote, which undergoes meiosis to form haploid spores. Examples: Volvox, Spirogyra, some species of Chlamydomonas.
Diplontic: the diploid sporophyte is the dominant, photosynthetic, independent phase; the gametophyte is reduced to a single to few cells. Examples: Fucus among algae, and all seed plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms).
Haplo-diplontic: both the gametophyte and the sporophyte are multicellular and often free-living but differ in dominance. In bryophytes the gametophyte dominates and the sporophyte depends on it; in pteridophytes the vascular sporophyte dominates and the prothallus is small and short-lived. Examples: Funaria, Dryopteris; among algae Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps.

pyq.q: Describe the sexual reproduction of bryophytes and explain why the sporophyte is said to be dependent.
pyq.answer: The main plant body of a bryophyte is the haploid gametophyte, which bears multicellular sex organs. The antheridium (male) produces biflagellate antherozoids; the flask-shaped archegonium (female) produces a single egg. Antherozoids are released into water and swim to the archegonium, where one fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote. The zygote does not undergo reduction division; it divides mitotically to form a multicellular sporophyte differentiated into foot, seta and capsule. The sporophyte has no roots and little or no photosynthetic tissue of its own; its foot stays embedded in the gametophyte, from which it draws water and nourishment, so it is not free-living but dependent. Spore mother cells in the capsule undergo meiosis to form haploid spores, which are dispersed and germinate into new gametophytes.

pyq.q: State three ways in which gymnosperms differ from pteridophytes.
pyq.answer: (i) Gymnosperms produce seeds (naked ovules develop into seeds after fertilisation); pteridophytes produce spores only and never form seeds. (ii) All gymnosperms are heterosporous, whereas most pteridophytes are homosporous (only Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous). (iii) In gymnosperms neither the male nor the female gametophyte is free-living; both are retained within the sporangia on the sporophyte, and the male gametophyte is reduced to a pollen grain. In pteridophytes the gametophyte (prothallus) is a free-living, photosynthetic plant. (iv) Gymnosperms transfer male gametes by a pollen tube after wind pollination and do not need external water for fertilisation; pteridophytes need water for the motile antherozoids to swim to the archegonium.

pyq.q: Describe the structure and reproduction of gymnosperms with a suitable example. Why are their seeds called naked?
pyq.answer:
Structure: Gymnosperms are medium to tall trees and shrubs (Cycas, Pinus, Cedrus, Sequoia). Roots are tap roots; Pinus roots have mycorrhiza and Cycas has coralloid roots with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Stems are unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). Leaves are simple or compound; Cycas has pinnate leaves that persist for a few years; conifers have needle-like leaves with thick cuticle and sunken stomata to reduce water loss and withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind.

Reproduction: Gymnosperms are heterosporous. Microspores and megaspores are produced in sporangia borne on sporophylls arranged spirally into compact cones (strobili). Male cones (microsporangiate strobili) carry microsporophylls with microsporangia, in which microspores develop into the highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain. Female cones (megasporangiate strobili) carry megasporophylls with ovules. In the ovule the megaspore mother cell, differentiated from the nucellus, divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one develops into a multicellular female gametophyte with two or more archegonia, retained within the megasporangium. In Pinus male and female cones are on the same tree; in Cycas on different trees. Neither gametophyte is free-living. Pollen grains are released and carried by wind to the opening of the ovule; a pollen tube carrying the male gametes grows to the archegonia and discharges them near the mouth. After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo and the ovule becomes the seed.

Naked seeds: The ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall; they lie exposed on the megasporophylls before and after fertilisation, so the seeds that form are not covered by a fruit. Hence gymnos (naked) sperma (seed). Draw a labelled Cycas or Pinus with male and female cones for the diagram mark.

pyq.q: Give an account of pteridophytes under the headings: habitat, plant body, reproduction, heterospory and classification.
pyq.answer:
Habitat: cool, damp, shady places; some in sandy soil. Used as medicines, soil binders and ornamentals. Evolutionarily the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissues (xylem and phloem).

Plant body: the main plant is a diploid sporophyte with true roots, stem and leaves and well-differentiated vascular tissue. Leaves are microphylls (Selaginella) or macrophylls (ferns).

Reproduction: sporophylls bear sporangia, sometimes packed into strobili or cones (Selaginella, Equisetum). Spore mother cells in the sporangia undergo meiosis to give spores, which germinate into the prothallus, a small, free-living, mostly photosynthetic gametophyte bearing antheridia and archegonia. Water is needed for the antherozoids to reach the archegonium. The zygote grows into the dominant sporophyte. Because the prothallus needs cool, damp, shady conditions and water for fertilisation, pteridophytes are restricted to narrow geographical regions.

Heterospory: most pteridophytes are homosporous; Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, forming megaspores (female gametophyte) and microspores (male gametophyte). The female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte and the embryo develops within it, a precursor to the seed habit.

Classification: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum). Add a labelled fern sporophyte with sori, or Selaginella with a strobilus, for the diagram.

pyq.q: With the help of labelled diagrams, describe the life cycle of Funaria and show how it illustrates alternation of generations.
pyq.answer:
Funaria is a moss. Its dominant phase is the haploid gametophyte, which has two stages. (1) The protonema, a creeping, green, branched filament, develops directly from the spore. (2) The leafy stage arises from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud: an upright slender axis with spirally arranged leaves, anchored by multicellular branched rhizoids. Antheridia and archegonia form at the apex of the leafy shoots. The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; the flask-shaped archegonium holds one egg. In a film of water the antherozoid reaches the archegonium and fertilisation forms the diploid zygote. Without meiosis, the zygote divides mitotically into the sporophyte, made of a foot embedded in the gametophyte, a seta and a capsule; it stays attached to and nourished by the gametophyte. Spore mother cells in the capsule undergo meiosis to produce haploid spores, which are dispersed by an elaborate mechanism and germinate into new protonema.

Alternation of generations: a multicellular haploid gametophyte (protonema and leafy plant), which produces gametes by mitosis, alternates with a multicellular diploid sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule), which produces spores by meiosis. Because both phases are multicellular and the gametophyte is dominant and independent while the sporophyte is short-lived and dependent, the cycle is haplo-diplontic. Diagrams: the leafy gametophyte with attached sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule, calyptra, rhizoids) and a cycle diagram marking fertilisation and meiosis.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Kelps are giant marine algae that can grow to 100 metres. They are attached to rocks by a holdfast, have a stalk called the stipe and a leaf-like frond. Their colour ranges from olive green to brown. Several kelps such as Laminaria are eaten, and their cell walls yield a substance widely used to thicken foods and cosmetics.
(i) To which class of algae do kelps belong, and which pigment gives them their colour?
(ii) Name the reserve food of kelps.
(iii) Name the substance obtained from their cell walls and one similar substance obtained from red algae.
(iv) Kelps show which pattern of life cycle? Name one other alga of the same class with a different pattern.
pyq.answer:
(i) Phaeophyceae (brown algae); the xanthophyll fucoxanthin, whose amount decides the colour. (1)
(ii) Complex carbohydrates, laminarin or mannitol. (1)
(iii) Algin, a hydrocolloid from brown algal cell walls; carrageen is the hydrocolloid from red algae (agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria also acceptable). (1)
(iv) Kelps are haplo-diplontic. Fucus, also a brown alga, is diplontic. (1)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student collected a small plant from a damp wall. It had a green creeping filamentous growth from which small upright leafy shoots arose, held to the wall by branched hairs. Some shoots carried a long stalk ending in a swollen capsule.
(i) Identify the group and name the creeping filamentous growth.
(ii) What are the branched hairs called, and are they unicellular or multicellular here?
(iii) Give the ploidy of a leaf cell of the shoot and of the spores in the capsule, and state where meiosis occurs.
(iv) Name the three parts of the structure carrying the capsule and state whether it can live independently.
pyq.answer:
(i) A moss (bryophyte); the creeping filamentous growth is the protonema, which develops from the spore. (1)
(ii) Rhizoids; in mosses they are multicellular and branched. (1)
(iii) Leaf cell: haploid (n), part of the gametophyte; spores: haploid (n). Meiosis occurs in the spore mother cells inside the capsule of the sporophyte. (1)
(iv) Foot, seta and capsule, together forming the sporophyte. It cannot live independently: it is attached to the gametophyte and draws nourishment from it. (1)

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is haplo-diplontic?
practice_mcq.explanation: Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps are the NCERT haplo-diplontic algae; Fucus is diplontic; Volvox and Spirogyra are haplontic.

practice_mcq.q: If a flowering plant has 2n = 24, the number of chromosomes in its endosperm cells is
practice_mcq.explanation: Endosperm is triploid: 3 × 12 = 36 (each gamete and polar nucleus carries 12).

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Numerical taxonomy: computers assigning numbers and codes to characters
practice_mcq.explanation: Numerical taxonomy uses computers and codes; cytotaxonomy uses chromosomes, chemotaxonomy uses chemicals, and phylogenetic (not artificial) systems use evolutionary relationships.

practice_mcq.q: The sporophyte of a liverwort consists of
practice_mcq.explanation: Foot, seta and capsule make up the bryophyte sporophyte; the other options describe a moss gametophyte, a brown alga and a fern.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following about angiosperm female gametophyte is correct?
practice_mcq.explanation: The typical embryo sac has 7 cells (egg, two synergids, three antipodals, one central cell) and 8 nuclei, because the central cell has two polar nuclei.

common_mistakes: Mixing up the stored foods: starch is green algae, mannitol and laminarin are brown algae, floridean starch is red algae. Writing 'starch' for all three loses the full mark on the comparison question.

Writing 'flagellated' anywhere for red algae. Rhodophyceae have no flagella; their spores and gametes are non-motile. Similarly, brown algal flagella are two, unequal and lateral, not equal and apical.
Confusing protonema (moss gametophyte stage, from the spore) with prothallus (fern gametophyte). Both are haploid, but the examiner wants the right name for the right plant.
Calling gemmae spores or saying they are formed by meiosis. Gemmae are multicellular, asexual, haploid buds of liverworts formed in gemma cups by mitosis.

Placing meiosis at gamete formation. In every plant, gametes are made by mitosis and meiosis makes spores: in the capsule (bryophytes), in the sporangia (pteridophytes), in microspore and megaspore mother cells (seed plants), or in the zygote (haplontic algae).

Saying the moss sporophyte is free-living or photosynthetic on its own. NCERT says it is attached to the gametophyte and derives nourishment from it; the reverse is true in pteridophytes, where the sporophyte is independent.

Answering 'seeds without fruit' alone for gymnosperms. The marking scheme wants ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall and exposed before and after fertilisation; mention the megasporophyll or cone as well.
Giving Sequoia as an angiosperm and Eucalyptus as a gymnosperm. Sequoia (giant redwood) is the tall gymnosperm; Eucalyptus (over 100 m) and Wolffia (microscopic) are the angiosperm size examples.
Marking Fucus haplontic because it is an alga. NCERT specifically names Fucus as diplontic, and Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia and kelps as haplo-diplontic.
Listing Spirulina as an alga used as food. Spirulina is a cyanobacterium (Monera) and is no longer in the NCERT text; the protein-supplement example is Chlorella.
strategy:
Treat this chapter as five groups plus one cycle, and learn each group under the same six headings: habitat, plant body, dominant phase and ploidy, sex organs, reproduction with the site of meiosis, and examples with economic importance. If you can fill this grid for algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms from memory, every question in the paper is a cell of the grid.

Spend the first sitting on Table 3.1 and the algal examples. Write the three rows out by hand until you can reproduce pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella and five examples per class without looking; this is the source of most 1-mark questions and of the standard 3-mark comparison. Add the reproduction vocabulary (isogamy, anisogamy, oogamy, zoospore) with its NCERT examples and the six economic uses.

The second sitting is bryophytes and pteridophytes together, because the paper loves to compare them: gametophyte-dominant versus sporophyte-dominant, protonema versus prothallus, gemmae versus sori, dependent versus independent sporophyte. Draw Funaria with its sporophyte and the fern with a sorus and prothallus, labelling ploidy on the drawing. Learn the four pteridophyte classes with one genus each and the heterospory paragraph word for word, since 'significance of heterospory' is a certain question.

The third sitting is gymnosperms, the most likely 5-mark question. Learn the vegetative adaptations, the two root associations, the cone structure, the fact that no gametophyte is free-living, and the wind-and-pollen-tube route to the archegonia; then be able to say in one line why they differ from angiosperms.

Finish with Section 3.6: draw the three life-cycle circles and attach every genus in the chapter to one of them. Then do NCERT exercises 2 and 4 (site of meiosis, ploidy list) as a timed test. In the exam, give 1-mark questions ten seconds each, write comparisons as two-column tables, and always add a labelled diagram to a 5-mark answer.
revision_checklist: I can name the three classification approaches (artificial, natural, phylogenetic) with Linnaeus and Bentham–Hooker, and define numerical taxonomy, cytotaxonomy and chemotaxonomy.
I can write Table 3.1 from memory: pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella and habitat for Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae, with five examples each.
I can define isogamy, anisogamy and oogamy with the NCERT examples (Ulothrix, Spirogyra; Chlamydomonas; Volvox, Fucus).
I can list six points of economic importance of algae, naming Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum, algin, carrageen, agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) and Chlorella.
I can explain why bryophytes are amphibians of the plant kingdom and describe the antheridium (biflagellate antherozoids) and the flask-shaped archegonium (one egg).
I can distinguish liverworts (Marchantia, thalloid, gemma cups, unicellular rhizoids) from mosses (protonema, leafy stage, multicellular rhizoids; Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum).
I can state the economic importance of bryophytes: Sphagnum peat and packing, pioneers on rock with lichens, preventing soil erosion.
I can describe the pteridophyte life cycle with prothallus, antheridia, archegonia, sporophylls, strobili and the site of meiosis, and name the four classes with a genus each.
I can define heterospory, give Selaginella and Salvinia, and explain why it is a precursor to the seed habit.

I can list the characteristics of gymnosperms: naked ovules, tap roots, mycorrhiza in Pinus, coralloid roots in Cycas, needle leaves with thick cuticle and sunken stomata, male and female strobili, no free-living gametophyte, wind pollination and pollen tube.
I know Sequoia is a gymnosperm, Wolffia the smallest angiosperm and Eucalyptus over 100 m the tallest angiosperm example.
I can give the ploidy of protonema, leaf cell of moss, prothallus, gemma, ovum, zygote of fern, meristem of monocot and primary endosperm nucleus.
I can state where meiosis occurs in a liverwort, moss, fern, gymnosperm and angiosperm.
I can describe haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic cycles with examples, including Fucus (diplontic) and Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps (haplo-diplontic).
I can draw and label Chlamydomonas, Laminaria, Marchantia, Funaria with sporophyte, a fern with sorus and prothallus, Selaginella, Cycas or Pinus, and the three life-cycle circles.
